Your turn. Write a or the: We have a garden. ___ garden is small.

Hi! Sure. Remember three things: start every sentence with a capital letter, always write I as a capital, and end with a full stop.

Hello! Yes. A small rule: at + clock time (at 7 o'clock), on + day (on Monday), in + month (in July).

Try this. Write in, on or at: My train leaves ___ 5 o'clock.
s751_PP_r2:
Hi! Of course. Quick rule: at for clock times, on for days, and in for months. Example: My holiday is in July.

Now try this one. Write in, on or at: They get married ___ April.
s757_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Use there is for one thing (There is a table.) and there are for two or more things (There are two chairs.).

Complete this sentence: "___ three windows in my room."
s763_PP_r2:
Hello! Yes. In English the order is: subject, then verb, then object. Example: Sam plays football. A time like "on Fridays" goes at the end.

Put these words in order: "plays / Sam / chess / on Mondays"
s769_PP_r2:
Hi! Sure. English order is subject + verb + object, and words like always, usually and often go before the main verb. Example: We usually have lunch at one.

Put these words in the right order: "often / my aunt / tea / makes"
s775_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Let's name things in the classroom. We can say "This is a ...". Example: This is a pen. This is a chair.

Complete this sentence: "I sit on a ___."
s781_PP_r2:
Hello! Good idea. With days we use on (on Monday), and with months we use in (in July).

Try this. Write in, on or at: They get married ___ April.
s787_PP_r2:
Hi! Sure. Days and months use different small words: on + day (I play tennis on Monday) and in + month (My holiday is in July).

Write in, on or at: I have my English class ___ Tuesday.
s793_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. To introduce someone, say "This is my ...". Then use he for a man or a boy, and she for a woman or a girl. Example: This is my sister. She is ten.

Complete: "This is my brother. ___ is twelve."

Complete: "I eat an ___ every morning." (a red or green fruit)

Hello! Sure. We use "in the + room" to say where we do things. Example: I cook dinner in the kitchen.

Complete: "My bed is in the ___."

Make this polite: "Give me a coffee."

Hello! Sure. Short adjectives take -er + than: fast becomes faster than. Long adjectives take more + than: more expensive than.

Complete: "Cairo is ___ (big) than Luxor."
s841_PP_r2:
Hi! Of course. Remember: short adjectives add -er (tall, taller), long adjectives use more (more beautiful), and we always add than. Example: A car is faster than a bike.

Complete: "This phone is ___ (expensive) than that one."
s847_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. We use and to add an idea, but to show a difference, and because to give a reason. Example: She is happy because it is Friday.

Join these two sentences with but: "The bus is cheap. It is slow."
s853_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Words like always, usually, sometimes and never go before the main verb. Example: My brother usually gets up at seven.

Put the word in the right place and write the sentence: "I have breakfast at home." (always)
s859_PP_r2:
Hi! Of course. These words go before the main verb: I never have coffee in the evening. And remember the -s with he, she and it.

Put the words in order: "gets up / she / at six / usually"
s865_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. For plans, we use am/is/are + going to + verb. Example: I'm going to visit my aunt tomorrow.

Correct this sentence: "I going to study tonight."
s871_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Use many with things we can count (eggs, bottles), and much with things we cannot count (rice, milk).

Write much or many: How ___ bottles are there?
s877_PP_r2:
Hi! Of course. We say many with countable nouns (How many eggs do we need?) and much with uncountable nouns (We don't have much rice).

Write much or many: How ___ rice do we need?
s883_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. For past questions, use did + subject + base verb. Example: What did you do last weekend? Did you go to the beach? (not "Did you went")

Make a question with did from these words: you / watch / TV / yesterday
s889_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Some verbs do not take -ed in the past. They change form, for example: go becomes went, buy becomes bought.

Write the past form of 'have': Yesterday I ___ a big lunch.
s895_PP_r2:
Hi! Of course. Irregular verbs change in the past and do not take -ed: see becomes saw, go becomes went. Example: I went to the market yesterday.

Write the past form of 'tell': Last night he ___ me a story.
s901_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. For regular verbs in the past, add -ed: play becomes played, visit becomes visited. Example: I watched a film last weekend.

Write the past form: Yesterday I ___ (visit) my grandmother.
s907_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. We use am/is/are + verb-ing for things happening now. Example: Two children are playing football.

Imagine a park. Write two sentences about what people are doing now.
s913_PP_r2:
Hi! Great. Present continuous is am/is/are + -ing. Use is for one person and are for two or more. Example: A man is walking in the park.

Complete: "Two girls ___ (sit) under a tree."
s919_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Use a or an with one countable thing (a sandwich, an apple), and some with things we cannot count (some water, some rice). We often use any in questions, for example: Do you have any tea?

Write a, an or some: "Can I have ___ water, please?"
s925_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. After he, she and it, we add -s to the verb. Example: I work. She works.

Write the correct form: My sister ___ (play) tennis on Sundays. (answer with only the verb)
s931_PP_r2:
Hi! Of course. With he, she and it, the verb gets -s. Verbs ending in -sh, -ch, -s, -x or -o get -es. Example: He teaches English.

Write the correct form: She ___ (watch) TV after dinner. (answer with only the verb)
s937_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Use has for things like hair and eyes (She has long hair), and is with adjectives (He is tall).

Complete: "My cousin ___ brown eyes." (has / have)

Hello! Sure. Use "How much is ...?" for one thing and "How much are ...?" for more than one. Example: How much is this hat?

Correct this question: "How much cost this hat?"

Hi! Of course. To ask for a size or a colour, say "Do you have this ... in ...?". Example: Do you have this jacket in blue?

Complete: "A chef works in a ___."

Hello! Sure. For weather, we use "It is + weather word". Example: It is sunny today.

Complete: "Take an umbrella. It is ___ today."
s967_PP_r2:
Hi! Of course. Our weather words are sunny, rainy, windy, cloudy, hot and cold. Remember to say "It is windy", not "It windy".

Complete: "My hat flew away! It is very ___."
